# WinDuo

The iPhone Duo fold effect, on any Windows laptop. No lid angle sensor required.

Live at https://winduo.baselashraf.com/
Source at https://github.com/BaselAshraf81/winduo

## Where this comes from

Apple's iPhone Duo, its first folding iPhone, blurs and stretches the interface
under perspective as the device folds between its two displays, so the change in
shape reads as continuous rather than as a hard cut. It tracks the hinge angle
the whole way and reverses if the motion reverses.

Mac Duo, an open-source Mac app by Makito, put the same effect on MacBook lids
within days of the announcement, driven by the lid angle sensor Apple has shipped
since the 2019 16-inch MacBook Pro.

WinDuo is the Windows version, and the first one that needs no angle sensor at
all. That matters because almost no laptop outside recent MacBooks has one, and
there is no software way to add one.

## What it does

Closing the lid makes the screen contents behave like a stiff sheet hinged along
the bottom edge of the display: the glass swings away underneath while the sheet
stays put in the room, so the picture leans back, converges under perspective,
blurs progressively toward its far edge, and dims.

## How the angle is measured, without a sensor

The webcam is mounted in the lid. A hinge is a single axis, so rotating the lid
rotates the camera by exactly the same amount, with no panning and no rolling.
Pure pitch translates the whole camera image vertically, which reduces the
measurement to one number per frame: how far the picture slid.

Phase correlation on a pair of downscaled greyscale frames recovers that in about
200 microseconds. Sensitivity is roughly 15 pixels per degree on a typical
webcam, so there is far more signal than the effect needs.

Adding those per-frame shifts up would drift without bound, so WinDuo never tries
to know the absolute angle. Whenever the lid holds still, that position becomes
zero, and the effect runs on travel away from it. Error therefore only
accumulates for the length of a single lid movement, one or two seconds, and a
fresh rest clears it. A consequence worth noting: it works with the laptop on a
desk, on a lap, or held at any starting position, because nothing depends on
where the hinge actually is.

Three checks keep it honest in a real room:

- Exposure is forced short while armed. A lid closing at 180 degrees per second
  covers 6 degrees inside one frame at 30 fps, and ordinary indoor exposure
  smears that across roughly 80 pixels, destroying the detail the correlator
  needs at the exact moment it is needed.
- Whole-machine movement is rejected. Picking the laptop up looks identical to
  closing the lid to anything measuring the frame as a whole, so both halves of
  the image must move together for a reading to be trusted.
- Losing the picture is reported rather than guessed at. A dark room, a covered
  camera, or another app holding the camera drive confidence to zero and the
  effect stays off.

Windows' own lid switch, GUID_LIDSWITCH_STATE_CHANGE, is the one piece of
hardware truth available. It gives no angle, but it says exactly when the lid is
shut, which anchors calibration at a known zero.

## Calibration

The camera measures pixels; converting to degrees needs one known angle, which no
amount of image processing can supply. A three-position wizard takes about twenty
seconds: the normal viewing position, where the user drags a silhouette to match;
roughly halfway, which fits a second-order term; and closed.

The relationship is not quite linear, for two reasons. Shift per degree grows
toward the edges of the frame because the projection is a tangent. And the camera
swings on an arc about 20 cm from the hinge, so a degree of closing also shifts it
around 3.5 mm sideways; against a wall one metre away that parallax adds about a
fifth to the apparent movement, and at three metres about a sixteenth. Since the
error depends on scene distance, the wizard asks the user to sit where they
normally sit rather than to measure anything.

## How it draws

The captured screen sits in one texture on a black margin with a mip pyramid over
it. One full-screen GLSL fragment pass per frame maps each screen pixel back
through the inverse perspective and takes a single sample at whatever mip level
matches the blur wanted at that height, so a 135-pixel blur costs the same as a
10-pixel one.

Two Windows specifics carry the approach. SetWindowDisplayAffinity with
WDA_EXCLUDEFROMCAPTURE keeps the overlay out of every screen capture API, without
which the overlay is captured, drawn into itself, and recurses; it requires
Windows 10 version 2004. And the overlay window is created once at startup and
never hidden, only faded, because a full-screen topmost window appearing
invalidates the display's duplication and recovering from that blocks for most of
a second.

Screen capture uses DXGI Desktop Duplication, with GDI copying as a fallback for
machines that refuse it.

## Honest limits

- Windows only. Capture and overlay both use Windows-only APIs. The angle
  estimation ports unchanged; the capture-exclusion API has no portable
  equivalent, which is the hard part of a Linux port.
- The camera indicator stays lit while running. The baseline has to exist before
  the lid starts moving. Frames are compared and discarded; nothing is recorded
  and nothing leaves the machine.
- Another application can claim the camera exclusively.
- Primary display only.
- Windows turns the screen off on lid close, so the effect only plays during the
  closing travel. macOS sleeps partway through too.
- Using a laptop in a moving vehicle produces false positives.
- Low light costs accuracy, and below a usable threshold the effect stays off.

## Technical facts

- Language: Python 3.11 or later. PyQt6 with OpenGL 3.3, OpenCV, numpy, dxcam.
- Licence: Apache 2.0, matching Mac Duo, which parts of the geometry, shader, and
  state machine are ported from. NOTICE lists which files.
- 116 automated tests, none of which need a camera, a display, or a lid.
- No telemetry, no account, no network access at runtime.
